analysis.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil rebounds as geopolitical risks linger
key_insights: Oil edged higher in early trading on 11 Nov 2026 after falling below $90/bbl the day before. Lingering US-Iran uncertainty supports prices despite bearish inventory data and expectations of better Middle East supply.

API data showed US crude stocks up 9m barrels last week against an expected draw of about 0.6m barrels. Cushing stocks rose 182k barrels, gasoline was broadly unchanged and distillates rose 1.5m barrels. Official EIA data is due later today.
The EIA lowered its 2026 US crude production forecast marginally to 13.86m b/d, about 200k b/d above 2025. Its 2027 forecast is unchanged at 14.3m b/d, implying growth of about 440k b/d.
The EIA expects US petroleum demand to be flat at 20.6m b/d in 2026 and rise to 20.9m b/d in 2027. It raised its 2027 gasoline and diesel price forecasts, citing continued tightness in fuel markets.

ADNOC reportedly cut the premium for December-loading Murban crude to $4/bbl, following price cuts from Saudi Aramco. The EIA expects most Middle East production outside Iran to recover to pre-conflict levels by mid-2027.
Reports of further damage to Russian energy infrastructure from Ukrainian drone attacks add supply risk. Several refineries have reportedly faced disruptions since late October.

ING sees developments in the Strait of Hormuz as the key driver for oil. Better regional flows would let more of the geopolitical premium unwind, while continued disruption leaves the market exposed to upside.

Gold edged higher on Wednesday after pressure from a stronger dollar and a sharp rise in US Treasury yields. Hotter-than-expected US inflation data reinforced expectations that the Fed could raise rates again in December.
Gold continues to find support around $4,000/oz from central-bank purchases and firm Asian physical demand, though uncertainty over the Fed's next move could keep prices volatile in the short term.

Speculative positioning in base metals remains subdued. Copper net longs fell by 1,094 lots to 34,449 lots, aluminium net longs fell by 430 lots to 86,442 lots, and zinc net longs fell by 463 lots to 27,361 lots, the lowest in more than a year.

sector_views.rationale: Bearish US inventory data and expected Middle East supply recovery weigh on oil. US-Iran uncertainty, Strait of Hormuz risk and Russian refinery disruptions provide support.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Larger than the expected draw of about 0.6m barrels, a bearish signal for oil.
A small build at the delivery hub.
Adds to the bearish inventory tone.
Marginally lowered but still about 200k b/d higher year-on-year.
Implies growth of about 440k b/d, so continued US supply growth.
Reinforced expectations of another Fed rate rise in December, a headwind for gold.

risk_factors: Renewed disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could push oil higher.
Further damage to Russian refineries and energy infrastructure.
A Fed rate rise in December and a stronger dollar with higher Treasury yields could pressure gold.
Subdued speculative positioning in base metals.

Aluminium net longs fell 430 lots to 86,442 lots, driven largely by a 10,218-lot rise in gross shorts.
Zinc net longs fell 463 lots to 27,361 lots, the lowest in more than a year.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict uncertainty continues to support oil prices.
Strait of Hormuz developments are the key driver for the oil market.
Ukrainian drone attacks have damaged Russian energy infrastructure, and several refineries have faced disruptions since late October.

tension_points.bull_case: US-Iran uncertainty, Strait of Hormuz risk and Russian refinery disruptions keep supply risk in the price, and continued disruptions leave the market vulnerable to renewed upside.
tension_points.bear_case: Bearish US inventory data, continued US supply growth and expected Middle East supply recovery weigh on prices, and better Hormuz flows would let the premium unwind.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An improvement in flows through the Strait of Hormuz would unwind more of the geopolitical premium.
